warmup.q: Fees are priced two ways: through an EnumMap<Method, FeeStrategy>, and through a switch expression over Method with no default. A teammate adds CRYPTO to the Method enum and builds. What happens?
options: The switch fails to compile; the map compiles and throws on the first crypto payment
The map fails to compile; the switch throws at runtime
Both compile, and crypto payments are charged 0
warmup.why: A switch expression over an enum with no default must cover every constant, so javac reports "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" right where the rule is missing. The map has no idea which keys should exist: EnumMap.get(CRYPTO) returns null, and calling .fee on it throws in production. That difference decides which shape fits which job.

sections.h: A strategy is a function you pass in
sections.html:
quotes.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor)) is the Strategy pattern in one line. sort owns the algorithm for putting things in order. The comparator is the one decision it leaves to you, passed in as an object. GoF Strategy is exactly that: a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, picked by the client.

In 1994 that meant an interface and a class per algorithm. Since Java 8, a lambda or a method reference is the class:

Java
record Quote(String psp, long feeMinor, long p95Millis) {}

Comparator<Quote> cheapest = Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor);
Comparator<Quote> cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenComparingLong(Quote::p95Millis);

quotes.sort(cheapestThenFastest);          // sort is the context; the comparator is the strategy
Kotlin
data class Quote(val psp: String, val feeMinor: Long, val p95Millis: Long)

val cheapest = compareBy<Quote> { it.feeMinor }
val cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenBy { it.p95Millis }

val ordered = quotes.sortedWith(cheapestThenFastest)   // sortedWith is the context; the comparator is the strategy

Comparator.comparing "accepts a function that extracts a Comparable sort key" and returns a comparator, and thenComparing chains a second one behind it. Nobody writes a class called FeeThenLatencyComparator any more. Kotlin's compareBy and thenBy do the same with function types, and any (Payment) -> Long already is a fee strategy, with no interface to declare.

The JDK hands you strategies in more places than sorting. ThreadPoolExecutor takes a RejectedExecutionHandler that decides what happens when its queue is full (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy and two more), and Collectors.groupingBy takes the function that decides which group each element joins. Each time, the library owns the loop and asks you for one decision.

A named type still helps in two cases. When the strategy has more than one method, such as a PSP client with authorize and refund, you have an interface with implementations, which is ordinary polymorphism. And a one-line @FunctionalInterface interface FeeStrategy { long fee(Payment p); } documents intent better than a bare ToLongFunction<Payment>, and reads better in stack traces.

Watch for state. A lambda that captures and changes a field is a strategy with hidden memory, and two threads sorting with it at once will corrupt each other's results. Keep strategies pure: input in, answer out.

try.title: Rank PSPs three ways
steps: Read StrategyDemo.java (or StrategyDemo.kt) and predict the three lines. Equal fees keep their original order, because the JDK's sort is stable.
Run it with the command below.
Add a fourth quote at the end of the list, new Quote("Bluefin", 25, 150) (PspQuote("Bluefin", 25, 150) in Kotlin). Predict all three lines again, then run.

code.title: StrategyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Three strategies for one decision: which PSP does the router try first? */ public class StrategyDemo { record Quote(String psp, long feeMinor, long p95Millis) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Quote> quotes = List.of( new Quote("Northpay", 30, 200), new Quote("Adyx", 25, 900), new Quote("Kestrel", 30, 120)); // each value is a complete strategy: no class per algorithm Map<String, Comparator<Quote>> policies = new LinkedHashMap<>(); policies.put("cheapest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor)); policies.put("fastest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::p95Millis)); policies.put("cheapest, then fastest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor).thenComparingLong(Quote::p95Millis)); // sorted() is the context: it owns the algorithm and asks the strategy one question policies.forEach((name, order) -> System.out.println(name + ": " + quotes.stream().sorted(order).map(Quote::psp).toList())); } }

With Bluefin: [Adyx, Bluefin, Northpay, Kestrel], [Kestrel, Bluefin, Northpay, Adyx] and [Bluefin, Adyx, Kestrel, Northpay]. Three algorithms, zero classes: each strategy is one expression.

sections.h: Refactor the if/else router, after pinning what it does
sections.html:
Every payments codebase has a method like LegacyRouter.fee: an if/else if chain on the payment method, with special cases added over the years. Before you touch it, pin what it does. Write a test that runs the old code and the new code over a grid of inputs (every method, amounts including 0 and 1, several countries) and asserts that they agree. Michael Feathers calls this a characterization test. It records today's behavior, bugs included, so the refactor can't change it by accident.

Choose the grid for its edges, not its size. Include amount 0, amount 1 (where integer division rounds a percentage down to nothing), the home country and a foreign one, and every enum constant. Those are the places where a refactored rule most often drifts by a cent.

Then pick one of two shapes:

Java
// open set: one lambda per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill
static final Map<Method, FeeStrategy> STRATEGIES = new EnumMap<>(Map.of(
        Method.CARD,   p -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000,
        Method.SEPA,   p -> 25,
        Method.WALLET, p -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000));

// closed set: one switch, checked by the compiler
static long fee(Payment p) {
    return switch (p.method()) {
        case CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000;
        case SEPA -> 25;
        case WALLET -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000;
    };
}
Kotlin
// open set: one lambda per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill
val strategies: Map<Method, (Payment) -> Long> = mapOf(
    Method.CARD to { p -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 },
    Method.SEPA to { _ -> 25L },
    Method.WALLET to { p -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 },
)

// closed set: one when, checked by the compiler
fun fee(p: Payment): Long = when (p.method) {
    Method.CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000
    Method.SEPA -> 25
    Method.WALLET -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000
}

A map of strategies suits an open set: methods loaded from config, PSP plug-ins, rules a merchant can switch on. A switch or when with no default suits a closed set you own, like your Method enum.

You see the difference the day someone adds CRYPTO to the enum. The switch stops compiling: "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values", or in Kotlin, "'when' expression must be exhaustive". The map compiles, ships, and throws on the first crypto payment: a NullPointerException from EnumMap.get in Java, or NoSuchElementException: Key CRYPTO is missing in the map from Kotlin's getValue. If you do choose a map for a closed set, add a startup check that every constant has an entry, so the failure moves from the first customer to the deploy.

Neither shape needs a class per payment method. The lambdas are the strategies.

try.title: Add a payment method and see who notices
steps: Run RouterDemo in either language: the map and the switch agree on all three methods.
Add CRYPTO to the enum (PayMethod). Predict which part fails, and when, then run.
Add the missing branch, case CRYPTO -> 0; in Java or PayMethod.CRYPTO -> 0 in Kotlin. Predict, then run again. Remove CRYPTO when you're done.

code.title: RouterDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.EnumMap; import java.util.Map; /** The same fee rules as a map of strategies and as a switch. Add a payment method and watch which one tells you. */ public class RouterDemo { enum PayMethod { CARD, SEPA, WALLET } record Pay(PayMethod method, long amountMinor) {} interface FeeStrategy { long fee(Pay p); } // open set: one lambda per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill static final Map<PayMethod, FeeStrategy> STRATEGIES = new EnumMap<>(Map.of( PayMethod.CARD, p -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000, PayMethod.SEPA, p -> 25, PayMethod.WALLET, p -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000)); // closed set: one switch, checked by the compiler static long feeSwitch(Pay p) { return switch (p.method()) { case CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000; case SEPA -> 25; case WALLET -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (PayMethod m : PayMethod.values()) { Pay p = new Pay(m, 10_000); System.out.printf("%-7s switch=%d", m, feeSwitch(p)); System.out.printf(" map=%d%n", STRATEGIES.get(m).fee(p)); } } }

alt.title: RouterDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l07 // The same fee rules as a map of strategies and as a when. Add a payment method and watch which one tells you. enum class PayMethod { CARD, SEPA, WALLET } data class Pay(val method: PayMethod, val amountMinor: Long) // open set: one function per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill private val strategies: Map<PayMethod, (Pay) -> Long> = mapOf( PayMethod.CARD to { p -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 }, PayMethod.SEPA to { _ -> 25L }, PayMethod.WALLET to { p -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 }, ) // closed set: one when, checked by the compiler private fun feeWhen(p: Pay): Long = when (p.method) { PayMethod.CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 PayMethod.SEPA -> 25 PayMethod.WALLET -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 } fun main() { for (m in PayMethod.entries) { val p = Pay(m, 10_000) print("%-7s when=%d".format(m, feeWhen(p))) println(" map=%d".format(strategies.getValue(m)(p))) } }

try.expect: With CRYPTO added, the build fails: javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'CRYPTO' branch or an 'else' branch. After you add the branch, three lines print and then CRYPTO switch=0 dies: Java throws NullPointerException because Map.get returned null, Kotlin throws NoSuchElementException: Key CRYPTO is missing in the map. The compiler found one gap; only a runtime crash found the other.

sections.h: Template Method: a skeleton with holes for subclasses
sections.html:
Every call to a PSP needs the same wrapping: start a timer, make the call, note the outcome, record it. Template Method puts that skeleton in a base class as a final method and leaves holes, called hooks, for subclasses to fill:

Java
abstract class OutboundCall<T> {
    public final T execute() {                         // the skeleton: subclasses can't change it
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return doCall();                           // hook 1: the varying step
        } finally {
            metrics.record(name(), System.nanoTime() - start);
        }
    }
    protected abstract String name();                  // hook 2
    protected abstract T doCall();
}

final class CaptureCall extends OutboundCall<String> {
    protected String name() { return "psp.capture"; }
    protected String doCall() { return psp.capture(authId); }
}
Kotlin
abstract class OutboundCall<T> {
    fun execute(): T {                                 // final by default in Kotlin: subclasses can't change it
        val start = System.nanoTime()
        try {
            return doCall()                            // hook 1: the varying step
        } finally {
            metrics.record(name(), System.nanoTime() - start)
        }
    }
    protected abstract fun name(): String              // hook 2
    protected abstract fun doCall(): T
}

class CaptureCall(private val authId: String) : OutboundCall<String>() {
    override fun name() = "psp.capture"
    override fun doCall() = psp.capture(authId)
}

The base class owns the order, and because execute is final, no subclass can skip the timer. The JDK uses the shape: to build an unmodifiable list, you extend AbstractList and write only get and size; the rest of List is a skeleton built on those two hooks.

Inheritance is the cost. A subclass depends on every detail of its parent, and a parent that changes when it calls its hooks can break subclasses it has never seen. That is the fragile base class problem. The sharpest edge is a base-class constructor that calls a hook. A subclass assigns its own fields only after the base constructor returns, so the hook runs on a half-built object. In Java, the field reads as null. In Kotlin, the same code reads null from private val psp: String, a property the type system promises is never null, and kotlinc compiles it without a warning.

Never call an overridable method from a constructor. Compute such values lazily, or pass them up to the base constructor as arguments.

try.title: Watch a hook run too early
steps: Read TemplateHookDemo.java (or .kt). The base constructor builds label by calling name(). Predict the label the template version prints.
Run it with the command below and compare the two versions.
Fix the template without changing ChargeCall: delete the label field and build the label inside execute() instead. Run again.

code.title: TemplateHookDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Template Method's sharpest edge, and the execute-around function that avoids it. */ public class TemplateHookDemo { // classic Template Method: a final skeleton with hooks for subclasses abstract static class OutboundCall { private final String label; OutboundCall() { label = "outbound " + name(); // calls a hook before the subclass has set its fields } final String execute() { // the skeleton System.out.println(" start " + label); try { return doCall(); } finally { System.out.println(" end " + label); } } abstract String name(); // hook abstract String doCall(); // hook } static final class ChargeCall extends OutboundCall { private final String psp; ChargeCall(String psp) { this.psp = psp; } // runs AFTER OutboundCall() has called name() String name() { return "charge via " + psp; } String doCall() { return "ch_1250"; } } // execute around: the same skeleton as a function; the varying step is a parameter static <T> T outbound(String name, Supplier<T> body) { System.out.println(" start " + name); try { return body.get(); } finally { System.out.println(" end " + name); } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("template: " + new ChargeCall("northpay").execute()); System.out.println("function: " + outbound("outbound charge via northpay", () -> "ch_1250")); } }

alt.title: TemplateHookDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l07 // Template Method's sharpest edge, and the execute-around function that avoids it. // classic Template Method: a skeleton with hooks for subclasses (Kotlin members are final unless open) abstract class OutboundCall { private val label = "outbound " + name() // calls a hook before the subclass has set its fields fun execute(): String { // the skeleton println(" start $label") try { return doCall() } finally { println(" end $label") } } abstract fun name(): String // hook abstract fun doCall(): String // hook } class ChargeCall(private val psp: String) : OutboundCall() { // psp is a non-null String... override fun name() = "charge via $psp" // ...and still reads as null here override fun doCall() = "ch_1250" } // execute around: the same skeleton as an inline function; the varying step is a lambda inline fun <T> outbound(name: String, body: () -> T): T { println(" start $name") try { return body() } finally { println(" end $name") } } fun main() { println("template: ${ChargeCall("northpay").execute()}") println("function: ${outbound("outbound charge via northpay") { "ch_1250" }}") }

try.expect: The template prints start outbound charge via null: name() ran inside the base constructor, before ChargeCall had assigned psp. Kotlin prints the same null from a property declared as non-null String, with no compiler warning. The function version prints charge via northpay. After the fix, the template prints it too, because name() now runs only when the object is complete.

sections.h: Execute around: pass the hole in as a function
sections.html:
The modern answer keeps the skeleton and drops the subclass. Write the skeleton as a function and take the varying step as a lambda:

Java
static <T> T timed(String name, Metrics metrics, Supplier<T> body) {
    long start = System.nanoTime();                    // setup
    try {
        return body.get();                             // the caller's code
    } finally {
        metrics.record(name, System.nanoTime() - start);   // teardown, always
    }
}

String captured = timed("psp.capture", metrics, () -> psp.capture(authId));
Kotlin
inline fun <T> timed(name: String, metrics: Metrics, body: () -> T): T {
    val start = System.nanoTime()                      // setup
    try {
        return body()                                  // the caller's code, inlined: no lambda object
    } finally {
        metrics.record(name, System.nanoTime() - start)    // teardown, always
    }
}

val captured = timed("psp.capture", metrics) { psp.capture(authId) }

This is execute around: the function runs the setup and the teardown, and calls your code in the middle. You use it every day. try-with-resources is execute around built into Java. Kotlin's standard library is full of it: use {} closes a resource, synchronized(lock) {} takes and releases a monitor, and measureTimeMillis {} times a block.

Kotlin makes the function version cheaper than Java's. The compiler copies the body of an inline function, lambda included, into each call site, so no lambda object is created, and a return inside the block returns from the enclosing function. Java's Supplier has a different limit: it can't throw checked exceptions, so wrapping an SDK call that throws IOException needs your own functional interface with a throws clause. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so timed { sdk.call() } just works.

Prefer the function. It composes (timed("psp.capture") { retrying(3) { psp.capture(id) } }), it needs no class per call site, and it can't hit the constructor trap, because there is no constructor. Keep Template Method for skeletons with many hooks, such as AbstractList, and make the template method final.

figure.caption: The same skeleton both ways. Template Method fills the hole with a subclass; execute around takes it as a lambda from the call site.

analogy: Strategy is the route setting on a satnav: fastest, shortest, avoid tolls. The satnav still plans the trip; you swap the one rule it uses to rank roads. Template Method is a printed form with blanks: the form fixes the order of the questions, and each department fills in its own answers. Execute around is a waffle iron: it heats up, times the bake and switches off, and you pour in whatever batter you like. The analogy breaks at the waffle iron's plug. A real appliance can't forget to switch off, but a hand-written execute-around function can, which is why the teardown belongs in a finally block.
world: Kafka already runs on strategies: the producer's partitioner.class names a Partitioner implementation, and the client calls it for every record. In your own services, the PSP router is the strategy you own: choose PSPs with a comparator over quotes, and price with a map or a switch depending on whether the set is yours. Temporal's RetryOptions is a back-off strategy passed as data. Execute around is the shape for everything that wraps a call in your Quarkus services: timing a PSP call, putting a payment id in the logging MDC for a block, running a block in a transaction. Write those as small higher-order functions, inline in Kotlin, instead of a base class every client must extend.
mistake: The most common mistake is adding default -> 0 (or else -> 0) to a switch over your own enum "to be safe". It feels defensive, and it silences the one check that mattered: when CRYPTO arrives, the compiler no longer lists the switches that need a rule, and crypto payments are priced at zero until finance notices. The map version has the same hole in a different place, a null lookup on the first crypto payment. For a closed set you own, leave the default out and let the build fail. Keep a default for open sets you don't control, such as config strings or vendor codes, and make it throw.

compare.title: An execute-around timer for SDK calls

java.title: Psp.java
java.html: // Supplier can't throw checked exceptions, so a wrapper for SDK calls needs its own interface @FunctionalInterface interface IoCall<T> { T call() throws IOException; } final class Psp { static <T> T timed(String name, Map<String, Long> metrics, IoCall<T> body) throws IOException { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return body.call(); } finally { metrics.merge(name, System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } static String captureOrNull(Map<String, Long> metrics, PspSdk sdk, String authId) throws IOException { String ref = timed("psp.capture", metrics, () -> sdk.capture(authId)); return ref.isEmpty() ? null : ref; // a lambda can't return from captureOrNull itself } }

kotlin.title: Psp.kt
kotlin.html: // inline: the block is pasted into the caller, so no lambda object and no checked-exception plumbing inline fun <T> timed(name: String, metrics: MutableMap<String, Long>, body: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return body() } finally { metrics.merge(name, System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } fun captureOrNull(metrics: MutableMap<String, Long>, sdk: PspSdk, authId: String): String? { val ref = timed("psp.capture", metrics) { sdk.capture(authId).ifEmpty { return null } // non-local return: leaves captureOrNull, the finally still records } return ref }

compare.note: The skeleton is identical: read the clock, run the caller's block, record in finally. Three things differ. Java's standard functional interfaces can't throw checked exceptions, so an SDK that throws IOException forces you to declare IoCall with a throws clause; Kotlin has no checked exceptions. Kotlin's inline copies timed and the block into each call site, so there is no lambda object, and return null inside the block returns from captureOrNull itself while the finally still runs. And an inline block may call suspend functions when the caller is a suspend function, which a Java lambda can't do. Neither language needs Template Method for this; the function is the whole pattern.

worked.title: Turn a back-off if/else into strategies, without changing behavior

steps.say: A retry helper reads the back-off policy name from config and decides the delay on every attempt. Spot two problems before reading on.
steps.code: // config: psp.backoff=exponential (or "fixed", "none") Duration delayBeforeRetry(String policy, int attempt) { if (policy.equals("fixed")) { return Duration.ofMillis(200); } else if (policy.equals("exponential")) { long ms = 100L << (attempt - 1); // 100, 200, 400, ... return Duration.ofMillis(Math.min(ms, 5_000)); } else if (policy.equals("none")) { return Duration.ZERO; } return Duration.ofMillis(200); // a typo in config silently means "fixed" }

alt.html: // config: psp.backoff=exponential (or "fixed", "none") fun delayBeforeRetry(policy: String, attempt: Int): Duration = if (policy == "fixed") { Duration.ofMillis(200) } else if (policy == "exponential") { val ms = 100L shl (attempt - 1) // 100, 200, 400, ... Duration.ofMillis(minOf(ms, 5_000)) } else if (policy == "none") { Duration.ZERO } else { Duration.ofMillis(200) // a typo in config silently means "fixed" }

steps.say: The policy is chosen again on every attempt, and a typo like exponentail quietly becomes "fixed". Fix neither yet. First pin today's behavior with a characterization test, so the refactor can't change a delay by accident.
steps.code: @ParameterizedTest @CsvSource({"fixed,1,200", "fixed,4,200", "exponential,1,100", "exponential,3,400", "exponential,9,5000", "none,2,0"}) void pinned(String policy, int attempt, long expectedMs) { assertThat(delayBeforeRetry(policy, attempt)).isEqualTo(Duration.ofMillis(expectedMs)); }

alt.html: @ParameterizedTest @CsvSource("fixed,1,200", "fixed,4,200", "exponential,1,100", "exponential,3,400", "exponential,9,5000", "none,2,0") fun pinned(policy: String, attempt: Int, expectedMs: Long) { assertThat(delayBeforeRetry(policy, attempt)).isEqualTo(Duration.ofMillis(expectedMs)) }

steps.say: Now give the decision a type with one method, and a factory for each policy. Each factory returns a lambda: a complete strategy.
steps.code: @FunctionalInterface interface Backoff { Duration delay(int attempt); // 1. one decision, one method static Backoff fixed(Duration d) { return attempt -> d; } static Backoff exponential(Duration base, Duration max) { return attempt -> { Duration d = base.multipliedBy(1L << (attempt - 1)); return d.compareTo(max) > 0 ? max : d; }; } Backoff NONE = attempt -> Duration.ZERO; }

alt.html: fun interface Backoff { fun delay(attempt: Int): Duration // 1. one decision, one method companion object { fun fixed(d: Duration) = Backoff { d } fun exponential(base: Duration, max: Duration) = Backoff { attempt -> minOf(base.multipliedBy(1L shl (attempt - 1)), max) } val NONE = Backoff { Duration.ZERO } } }

steps.say: Choose the strategy once, at startup. Here a default is right, because config strings are an open set you don't control, and it throws, so a typo fails the deploy. Point the pinned test at fromConfig(policy).delay(attempt): it still passes.
steps.code: static Backoff fromConfig(String name) { // 2. choose once, at startup return switch (name) { case "fixed" -> Backoff.fixed(Duration.ofMillis(200)); case "exponential" -> Backoff.exponential(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(5)); case "none" -> Backoff.NONE; default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown psp.backoff: " + name); // 3. a typo fails the deploy }; } Backoff backoff = fromConfig(config.backoff()); // 4. the retry loop calls backoff.delay(n)

lab.title: Refactor the fee router twice, and replace a template with a function
steps: Read Method, Payment and LegacyRouter. They are given, and LegacyRouter.fee is the specification. Run the tests: all eight fail.

drill.title: A retry wrapper from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write retrying(attempts, body) as an execute-around function: it runs body up to attempts times, returns the first success, and rethrows the last failure. In Kotlin make it inline. Then say which PSP call you would never pass to it without an idempotency key.

answer.html: static <T> T retrying(int attempts, Supplier<T> body) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return body.get(); // the caller's step, run again on failure } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw last; // never pass a charge without an idempotency key }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: inline fun <T> retrying(attempts: Int, body: () -> T): T { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return body() // non-local return from retrying } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e } } throw last!! // never pass a charge without an idempotency key }

recap: Strategy is an algorithm the client picks and passes in. In modern Java and Kotlin, a lambda, method reference or function type is the strategy; Comparator.comparing is the JDK's own example.
Before refactoring an if/else chain, pin its behavior with a characterization test over a grid of inputs.
Use a map of strategies for open sets (config, plug-ins) and a switch or when with no default for closed sets you own. A missing map entry fails at runtime; a missing case fails to compile.
Template Method is a final skeleton in a base class with hooks for subclasses. Never call a hook from a constructor: the subclass's fields are still unset, even Kotlin non-null vals.
Execute around replaces most Template Methods: the skeleton is a function and the varying step is a lambda, as in try-with-resources, use, synchronized and measureTimeMillis.
Kotlin inline makes execute around free of lambda objects and allows non-local return; Java's Supplier can't throw checked exceptions.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Should our fee rules live in a Map<Method, FeeStrategy> or in a switch over Method?" Explain how you decide, and what each version does on the day someone adds a new payment method.
explain.answer: It depends on who owns the set of keys. If the set is closed and ours, like the Method enum, I use a switch (or when) with no default. When someone adds CRYPTO, the build fails at every switch that needs a rule, so nobody can ship without deciding the crypto fee. If the set is open, because rules come from config or plug-ins or merchants switch them on, a map of strategies fits, since the code can't know the keys at compile time. The map's weakness is that a missing entry only shows up at runtime: EnumMap.get returns null and the first crypto payment fails. If we use a map for an enum anyway, we add a startup check that every constant has an entry, so the deploy fails instead of a customer's payment. Either way, I'd pin the current behavior with a parity test against the old code before changing anything.

deeper.html:
Strategy and State have the same structure: an object holds an interface and delegates to it. The difference is who chooses. The client picks a strategy and it stays put. A state object, or a transition function, picks the next state itself as events arrive. Lesson 9 of this track, State and Chain of Responsibility, builds the payment lifecycle that way.

Java can do execute around without lambdas. Make the setup a constructor and the teardown close(), and try-with-resources does the rest: try (var t = metrics.timer("psp.capture")) { return psp.capture(id); }. This form lets checked exceptions pass through untouched and needs no functional interface, which is why many tracing and metrics libraries offer a closeable span or timer. The cost is that the caller must remember the try.

Kotlin's inline has limits worth knowing. An inlined lambda can't be stored or passed to a non-inline function, because it doesn't exist as an object. Mark such a parameter noinline. If the lambda runs in another context (a different thread, a callback), mark it crossinline, which forbids non-local returns inside it. And large inline functions grow every call site, so keep them small: the skeleton inline, the heavy lifting in a normal function it calls.

Spring's JdbcTemplate and TransactionTemplate carry the pattern's name, but they take your code as a callback, which is the execute-around shape from this lesson. The name stuck from an era when callbacks needed anonymous inner classes.
